claim: Protein kinases comprise 1.7% of the human genome.
source: Protein kinases are one of the largest druggable protein families comprising 1.7% of the human genome and play essential roles in regulating diverse eukaryotic cell signaling pathways (Manning et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Manning et al., 2002.

claim: Doublecortin-like kinases (DCLKs) are members of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CAMK) clade of serine-threonine kinases.
source: The doublecortin-like kinases (DCLKs) are understudied members of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CAMK) clade of serine-threonine kinases (Agulto et al., 2021; Bayer and Schulman, 2019; Gógl et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: There are three distinct paralogs of DCLK (1, 2, and 3).
source: There are three distinct paralogs of DCLK (1, 2, and 3), the last of which is annotated as a 'dark' kinase due to the lack of information pertaining to its function (Berginski et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: DCLK3 is annotated as a 'dark' kinase due to the lack of information pertaining to its function.
source: There are three distinct paralogs of DCLK (1, 2, and 3), the last of which is annotated as a 'dark' kinase due to the lack of information pertaining to its function (Berginski et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Human DCLK1 was initially identified in 1999.
source: Human DCLK1 (also known as DCAMKL1) was initially identified in 1999 (Sossey-Alaoui and Srivastava, 1999), followed by the cloning of human DCLK2 and -3 paralogs (Ohmae et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Human DCLK2 and -3 paralogs were cloned after DCLK1.
source: Human DCLK1 (also known as DCAMKL1) was initially identified in 1999 (Sossey-Alaoui and Srivastava, 1999), followed by the cloning of human DCLK2 and -3 paralogs (Ohmae et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Full-length DCLK proteins contain N-terminal doublecortin-like (DCX) domains.
source: Full-length DCLK proteins contain N-terminal doublecortin-like (DCX) domains, microtubule-binding elements that play a role in microtubule dynamics, neurogenesis, and neuronal migration (Couillard-Despres et al., 2005; Horesh et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: DCX domains are microtubule-binding elements that play a role in microtubule dynamics, neurogenesis, and neuronal migration.
source: Full-length DCLK proteins contain N-terminal doublecortin-like (DCX) domains, microtubule-binding elements that play a role in microtubule dynamics, neurogenesis, and neuronal migration (Couillard-Despres et al., 2005; Horesh et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: DCLKs are upregulated in a variety of cancer pathologies.
source: DCLKs have garnered much interest as disease biomarkers, since they are upregulated in a variety of cancer pathologies (Cheng et al., 2022a; Gao et al., 2016; Westphalen et al., 2017), as well as neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease (Galvan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: DCLKs are upregulated in neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease.
source: DCLKs have garnered much interest as disease biomarkers, since they are upregulated in a variety of cancer pathologies (Cheng et al., 2022a; Gao et al., 2016; Westphalen et al., 2017), as well as neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease (Galvan et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The catalytic domain of DCLKs adopts a bi-lobal fold.
source: Like all protein kinases, the catalytic domain of DCLKs adopts a bi-lobal fold (Gógl et al., 2019), with an N-terminal ATP-binding lobe and C-terminal substrate-binding region.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The catalytic domain of DCLKs has an N-terminal ATP-binding lobe and C-terminal substrate-binding region.
source: Like all protein kinases, the catalytic domain of DCLKs adopts a bi-lobal fold (Gógl et al., 2019), with an N-terminal ATP-binding lobe and C-terminal substrate-binding region.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Canonical elements within the two lobes of the kinase domain include the DFG motif, a Lys-Glu salt bridge, Gly-rich loop, and ATP-binding pocket.
source: Canonical elements within the two lobes include the DFG motif, a Lys-Glu salt bridge that is associated with the active conformation, Gly-rich loop, and ATP-binding pocket, which are all critical elements for catalysis.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Many protein kinases, including CAMKs, tyrosine kinases, and AGCs, have unique N-terminal and C-terminal extensions that flank the catalytic lobes.
source: Many protein kinases, including CAMKs, tyrosine kinases, and AGCs, elaborate on these core elements with unique N-terminal and C-terminal extensions that flank these catalytic lobes (Kannan et al., 2007; Yeon et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2015a; Yeung et al., 2021; Kwon et al., 2018), allowing them to function as allosteric regulators of catalytic activity (Gógl et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations.

claim: N-terminal and C-terminal extensions in protein kinases function as allosteric regulators of catalytic activity.
source: Many protein kinases, including CAMKs, tyrosine kinases, and AGCs, elaborate on these core elements with unique N-terminal and C-terminal extensions that flank these catalytic lobes (Kannan et al., 2007; Yeon et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2015a; Yeung et al., 2021; Kwon et al., 2018), allowing them to function as allosteric regulators of catalytic activity (Gógl et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: CAMKs can exist in an active-like structural conformation yet remain catalytically inactive.
source: Indeed, CAMKs are archetypal examples of kinases that can exist in an active-like structural conformation, yet still remain catalytically inactive (Gógl et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: CAMKs have unique C-terminal tails that are capable of blocking ATP or substrate binding.
source: This is in large part due to the presence of unique C-terminal tails that are capable of blocking ATP or substrate binding in well-studied kinases such as CAMK1 and CAMKII.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: In canonical CAMKs, autoinhibition may be released upon Ca2+/calmodulin (CaM) interaction with the CAMK C-tail.
source: In canonical CAMKs, autoinhibition may be released upon Ca2+/calmodulin (CaM) interaction with the CAMK C-tail, which makes the substrate-binding pocket and enzyme active site accessible (Rellos et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: In CAMKII, the N- and C-terminal segments flanking the kinase domain are variable in length across different isoforms.
source: In CAMKII, the N- and C-terminal segments flanking the kinase domain are variable in length across different isoforms and the level of kinase autoinhibition or autoactivation has been reported to be dependent on the linker length (Bhattacharyya et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The level of kinase autoinhibition or autoactivation in CAMKII is dependent on the linker length.
source: In CAMKII, the N- and C-terminal segments flanking the kinase domain are variable in length across different isoforms and the level of kinase autoinhibition or autoactivation has been reported to be dependent on the linker length (Bhattacharyya et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The CAMKII C-tail can be organized into an autoregulatory domain and an intrinsically disordered association domain.
source: The CAMKII C-tail can be organized into an autoregulatory domain and an intrinsically disordered association domain.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The autoregulatory domain of CAMKII serves as a pseudosubstrate, which physically blocks the substrate-binding pocket until it is competed away by CaM.
source: The autoregulatory domain also serves as a pseudosubstrate, which physically blocks the substrate-binding pocket until it is competed away by CaM (Hudmon and Schulman, 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: The autoregulatory pseudosubstrate of CAMKII can be phosphorylated.
source: Notably, this autoregulatory pseudosubstrate can be phosphorylated (Rellos et al., 2010), and phosphorylation of the C-tail makes CAMKII insensitive to CaM binding.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Phosphorylation of the C-tail makes CAMKII insensitive to CaM binding.
source: Notably, this autoregulatory pseudosubstrate can be phosphorylated (Rellos et al., 2010), and phosphorylation of the C-tail makes CAMKII insensitive to CaM binding.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Several CAMK group kinases share autoinhibitory activity via interactions between Ca2+/CaM binding domains and the C-terminal tail.
source: Across the CAMK group, several other kinases share autoinhibitory activity via interactions between Ca2+/CaM binding domains and the C-terminal tail (Huse and Kuriyan, 2002; Wayman et al., 2008), and a major feature of these kinases is variation in the tail length across the distinct genetic isoforms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: A major feature of CAMK group kinases is variation in the tail length across the distinct genetic isoforms.
source: Across the CAMK group, several other kinases share autoinhibitory activity via interactions between Ca2+/CaM binding domains and the C-terminal tail (Huse and Kuriyan, 2002; Wayman et al., 2008), and a major feature of these kinases is variation in the tail length across the distinct genetic isoforms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The human genome encodes four distinct DCLK1 isoforms, termed DCLK1.1–1.4.
source: The human genome encodes four distinct DCLK1 isoforms, termed DCLK1.1–1.4 in UniProt (Table 1, Figure 1; Omori et al., 1998), which display differential activity- and tissue-specific expression profiles.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation and references to Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Human DCLK1 isoforms display differential activity- and tissue-specific expression profiles.
source: The human genome encodes four distinct DCLK1 isoforms, termed DCLK1.1–1.4 in UniProt (Table 1, Figure 1; Omori et al., 1998), which display differential activity- and tissue-specific expression profiles.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Human DCLK1.1 is expressed in a variety of tissues, but is enriched in cells derived from the fetal and adult brain.
source: Human DCLK1.1 (also known as DCLK1 alpha) is expressed in a variety of tissues, but is enriched in cells derived from the fetal and adult brain, whereas DCLK1.2 (also known as DCLK1 beta) is expressed exclusively in the embryonic brain (Matsumoto et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: DCLK1.2 is expressed exclusively in the embryonic brain.
source: Human DCLK1.1 (also known as DCLK1 alpha) is expressed in a variety of tissues, but is enriched in cells derived from the fetal and adult brain, whereas DCLK1.2 (also known as DCLK1 beta) is expressed exclusively in the embryonic brain (Matsumoto et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: DCLK1.3 and DCLK1.4 lack tandem microtubule-binding DCX domains.
source: DCLK1.3 and DCLK1.4, which lack tandem microtubule-binding DCX domains (Figure 1) but are otherwise identical to DCLK1.1 and DCLK1.2, respectively, are also highly expressed in the brain.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1.

claim: DCLK1.3 and DCLK1.4 are highly expressed in the brain.
source: DCLK1.3 and DCLK1.4, which lack tandem microtubule-binding DCX domains (Figure 1) but are otherwise identical to DCLK1.1 and DCLK1.2, respectively, are also highly expressed in the brain.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Autophosphorylation of Thr 688 in DCLK1.2 blunts kinase activity.
source: Mechanistically, autophosphorylation of Thr 688, which is present only in the C-tail of DCLK1.2 (and DCLK1.4), blunts kinase activity and subsequently inhibits phosphorylation of the N-terminal DCX domain and thus drives DCLK microtubule association in cells (Agulto et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Thr 688 is present only in the C-tail of DCLK1.2 and DCLK1.4.
source: Mechanistically, autophosphorylation of Thr 688, which is present only in the C-tail of DCLK1.2 (and DCLK1.4), blunts kinase activity and subsequently inhibits phosphorylation of the N-terminal DCX domain and thus drives DCLK microtubule association in cells (Agulto et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Autophosphorylation of Thr 688 in DCLK1.2 inhibits phosphorylation of the N-terminal DCX domain.
source: Mechanistically, autophosphorylation of Thr 688, which is present only in the C-tail of DCLK1.2 (and DCLK1.4), blunts kinase activity and subsequently inhibits phosphorylation of the N-terminal DCX domain and thus drives DCLK microtubule association in cells (Agulto et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Autophosphorylation of Thr 688 in DCLK1.2 drives DCLK microtubule association in cells.
source: Mechanistically, autophosphorylation of Thr 688, which is present only in the C-tail of DCLK1.2 (and DCLK1.4), blunts kinase activity and subsequently inhibits phosphorylation of the N-terminal DCX domain and thus drives DCLK microtubule association in cells (Agulto et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Deletion of the C-tail or mutation of Thr 688 restores DCLK1.2 kinase activity.
source: Consistently, deletion of the C-tail or mutation of Thr 688 restores DCLK1.2 kinase activity, subsequently leading to DCX domain phosphorylation and the abolition of microtubule binding.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Deletion of the C-tail or mutation of Thr 688 leads to DCX domain phosphorylation and the abolition of microtubule binding.
source: Consistently, deletion of the C-tail or mutation of Thr 688 restores DCLK1.2 kinase activity, subsequently leading to DCX domain phosphorylation and the abolition of microtubule binding.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: The length and sequence of the C-tail varies across the DCLK1 isoforms.
source: The length and sequence of the C-tail varies across the DCLK1 isoforms; however, how these variations contribute to isoform-specific functions and how they emerged during the course of evolution is not known.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of 36 DCLK sequences generated four distinct clades: pre-metazoan DCLK, metazoan DCLK3, vertebrate DCLK2, and vertebrate DCLK1.
source: The analysis generated four distinct clades: pre-metazoan DCLK, metazoan DCLK3, vertebrate DCLK2, and vertebrate DCLK1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on phylogenetic analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: Pre-metazoan DCLK sequences were the most ancestral and showed no DCLK diversity.
source: The pre-metazoan DCLK sequences were the most ancestral and showed no DCLK diversity, suggesting the DCLK expansion and diversification correlated with the evolution of multicellular organisms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: DCLK expansion and diversification correlated with the evolution of multicellular organisms.
source: The pre-metazoan DCLK sequences were the most ancestral and showed no DCLK diversity, suggesting the DCLK expansion and diversification correlated with the evolution of multicellular organisms.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is inferred from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: DCLK3 is the most ancestral within the metazoan expansion of DCLK.
source: Within the metazoan expansion of DCLK, DCLK3 is the most ancestral and can be broken down into two sub-clades: protostome DCLK3 and deuterostome DCLK3.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: DCLK3 can be broken down into two sub-clades: protostome DCLK3 and deuterostome DCLK3.
source: Within the metazoan expansion of DCLK, DCLK3 is the most ancestral and can be broken down into two sub-clades: protostome DCLK3 and deuterostome DCLK3.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Within invertebrates, only two DCLK paralogs were present.
source: Within invertebrates, only two DCLK paralogs were present, one that was identified as a DCLK3 ortholog and another that was not clearly defined as either DCLK1 or DCLK2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The diversification into DCLK1 and DCLK2 paralogs from an ancestral DCLK1/2-like paralog occurred after the divergence of invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: This suggests that the diversification into DCLK1 and DCLK2 paralogs from an ancestral DCLK1/2-like paralog occurred after the divergence of invertebrates and vertebrates, which is further supported by the monophyletic DCLK1 and DCLK2 clades in vertebrates (bootstrap value: 99).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is inferred from phylogenetic analysis with bootstrap support.

claim: The expansion of DCLK in metazoans and the diversification of DCLK1 and DCLK2 within vertebrates correlates with the length and sequence similarity of the C-terminal tail.
source: Interestingly, the expansion of DCLK in metazoans and the diversification of DCLK1 and DCLK2 within vertebrates correlates well with the length and sequence similarity of the C-terminal tail, which also varies between the different DCLK1 splice variants (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Within both protostome and deuterostome DCLK3, the length of the C-terminal tail is ~50 residues or less.
source: Within both protostome and deuterostome DCLK3, the length of the C-terminal tail is ~50 residues or less.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The tail lengths of vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2 are ~100 residues long.
source: This is in marked contrast to the tail lengths of vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2, which are ~100 residues long.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence analysis.

claim: DCLK3 predominantly contains only a single N-terminal doublecortin domain (DCX).
source: In addition to the C-terminal tail, an analysis of the domain organization of these DCLKs reveals that DCLK3 predominantly contains only a single N-terminal doublecortin domain (DCX), whereas invertebrate DCLKs, and vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2 predominantly contain two DCX domains at the N-terminus of the long isoforms (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Invertebrate DCLKs, and vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2 predominantly contain two DCX domains at the N-terminus of the long isoforms.
source: In addition to the C-terminal tail, an analysis of the domain organization of these DCLKs reveals that DCLK3 predominantly contains only a single N-terminal doublecortin domain (DCX), whereas invertebrate DCLKs, and vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2 predominantly contain two DCX domains at the N-terminus of the long isoforms (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: A putative active site-binding motif, VSVI, is conserved within vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2.
source: In addition, we identified a putative active site-binding motif, VSVI, and a phosphorylatable threonine conserved within vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2, which is absent in all other DCLK sequences, including invertebrate DCLK1/2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence analysis.

claim: A phosphorylatable threonine is conserved within vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2, which is absent in all other DCLK sequences, including invertebrate DCLK1/2.
source: In addition, we identified a putative active site-binding motif, VSVI, and a phosphorylatable threonine conserved within vertebrate DCLK1 and DCLK2, which is absent in all other DCLK sequences, including invertebrate DCLK1/2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The DCLK1/2 tail extensions are employed for vertebrate-specific regulatory functions.
source: This raises the possibility that the DCLK1/2 tail extensions are employed for vertebrate-specific regulatory functions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is speculative based on sequence analysis.

claim: It was only in the human DCLK1 gene that definitive evidence for ΔDCLK1.1 and ΔDCLK1.2 variants were found.
source: Interestingly, it was only in the human DCLK1 gene that definitive evidence for ΔDCLK1.1 and ΔDCLK1.2 variants were found (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Purified DCLK1.1 and DCLK1.2 isoforms are monomeric in solution.
source: Analytical SEC revealed that purified DCLK1.1 and DCLK1.2 isoforms are monomeric in solution (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by analytical SEC data in figure supplements.

claim: DCLK1.1351-689 efficiently phosphorylates a DCLK1 substrate peptide.
source: We evaluated catalytic activity for DCLK1.1351-689 using a validated peptide phosphorylation assay (Figure 3C), which revealed efficient phosphorylation of a DCLK1 substrate peptide.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: The KM[ATP] for peptide phosphorylation by DCLK1.1351-689 was close to 20 µM in the presence of Mg2+ ions.
source: The KM[ATP] for peptide phosphorylation was close to 20 µM in the presence of Mg2+ ions (Figure 3C, left panel), similar to values measured for other Ser/Thr kinases that are autophosphorylated and active after expression from bacteria (Byrne et al., 2020b).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C and a citation.

claim: DCLK-dependent peptide phosphorylation was completely blocked by prior incubation with the chemical inhibitor DCLK1-IN-1.
source: DCLK-dependent peptide phosphorylation was completely blocked (Figure 3C, right panel) by prior incubation of the reaction mixture (containing 1 mM ATP) with the chemical inhibitor DCLK1-IN-1, as expected (Ferguson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3C and a citation.

claim: DCLK1 was stabilized by 2.1°C upon incubation with an excess of Mg:ATP.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, DCLK1 was stabilized by 2.1°C upon incubation with an excess of Mg:ATP, and this protective effect was completely blocked by mutation of Asp 533 (of the conserved DFG motif) to Ala, consistent with canonical ATP interaction in the nucleotide-binding site.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: The protective effect of Mg:ATP on DCLK1 thermal stability was completely blocked by mutation of Asp 533 to Ala.
source: As shown in Figure 3D, DCLK1 was stabilized by 2.1°C upon incubation with an excess of Mg:ATP, and this protective effect was completely blocked by mutation of Asp 533 (of the conserved DFG motif) to Ala, consistent with canonical ATP interaction in the nucleotide-binding site.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3D.

claim: Prior incubation with DCLK1-IN-1, LRRK2-IN-1, XMD8-92, and XMD8-85 led to marked protection from thermal unfolding of DCLK1.1351-689.
source: Prior incubation with DCLK1-IN-1, LRRK2-IN-1, the benzopyrimidodiazipinones XMD8-92 and XMD8-85, which have been reported to potently (though not specifically) inhibit DCLK1 activity (Patel et al., 2021), led to marked protection from thermal unfolding (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and a citation.

claim: The negative control compound DCLK1-Neg was ineffective in stabilizing DCLK1.
source: Consistently, the negative control compound DCLK1-Neg (Ferguson et al., 2020) was ineffective in stabilizing DCLK1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation.

claim: Isoforms 1 and 2 of DCLK1 differ in C-terminal tail length due to variations in exon splicing.
source: Isoforms 1 and 2 differ in C-terminal tail length due to variations in exon splicing (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Human DCLK1.1 contains an additional exon (exon 16) that is not spliced in DCLK1.2.
source: Further examination of the intron and exon boundaries indicates that human DCLK1.1 contains an additional exon (exon 16) that is not spliced in DCLK1.2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Exon 16 is spliced with exon 17 with a phase 2 intron in DCLK1.1, which introduces a shift in the reading frame and an earlier translated stop codon (UGA) in exon 17.
source: Exon 16 is spliced with exon 17 with a phase 2 intron, which introduces a shift in the reading frame and an earlier translated stop codon (UGA) in exon 17 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: In DCLK1.2, exon 15 is spliced with exon 17, with a non-disruptive phase 0 intron, resulting in the full translation of exon 17.
source: In DCLK1.2, exon 15 is spliced with exon 17, with a non-disruptive phase 0 intron, resulting in the full translation of exon 17.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Alternative splicing introduces multiple indels and results in the insertion of a phosphorylatable threonine (T688) in DCLK1.2 that is absent in the DCLK1.1 variant.
source: These changes introduce multiple indels (insertions and deletions) and result in the insertion of a phosphorylatable threonine (T688) (Agulto et al., 2021) in DCLK1.2 that is absent in the DCLK1.1 variant (Figure 4B–C), suggesting a possible exon duplication for adaptive regulation of DCLK1 function by phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B-C and a citation.

claim: DCLK1.2 was some 14°C more stable than DCLK1.1 when comparing DCLK1.1short and DCLK1.2short.
source: When contrasting DCLK1.1short and DCLK1.2short which do not differ in size or tail length but encode unique sets of amino acids in their partially truncated C-tail as a result of alternative splicing (Figure 4), we observed that DCLK1.2 was some 14°C more stable than DCLK1.1 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Both DCLK1.1 short and long exhibited only subtle changes in thermal stability compared to DCLK1cat.
source: When compared with DCLK1cat, both DCLK1.1 short and long exhibited only subtle changes in thermal stability (Figure 5C and E), whereas both DCLK1.2 proteins (DCLK1.2short and DCLK1.2long) were significantly stabilized (relative ΔTm >16°C, Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5C and E.

claim: Both DCLK1.2 proteins (DCLK1.2short and DCLK1.2long) were significantly stabilized (relative ΔTm >16°C) compared to DCLK1cat.
source: When compared with DCLK1cat, both DCLK1.1 short and long exhibited only subtle changes in thermal stability (Figure 5C and E), whereas both DCLK1.2 proteins (DCLK1.2short and DCLK1.2long) were significantly stabilized (relative ΔTm >16°C, Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The IBS (between 682 and 688) is stably docked in the ATP-binding pocket in DCLK1.2 and an alpha-helical conformation is maintained during the microsecond time scale across different replicates.
source: In particular, the IBS (between 682 and 688) is stably docked in the ATP-binding pocket in DCLK1.2 and an alpha-helical conformation is maintained during the microsecond time scale across different replicates (Figure 5I, bottom).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 5I.

claim: The IBS is more unstable in DCLK1.1, as indicated by high thermal fluctuations and a lack of secondary structure propensity.
source: In contrast, the IBS is more unstable in DCLK1.1, as indicated by high thermal fluctuations and a lack of secondary structure propensity (Figure 5I, top).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 5I.

claim: The helical conformation of the IDS in DCK1.2 is maintained during the simulation due, in part, to a capping interaction with Thr 687.
source: The helical conformation of the IDS in DCK1.2 is maintained during the simulation due, in part, to a capping interaction with Thr 687, which is absent in DCLK1.1 due to the alternative splicing event detailed above.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: Lys 692 in DCLK1.2 anchors the tail to the catalytic domain through directional salt bridges with the conserved aspartates (Asp 511 and Asp 533) in the HRD and DFG motifs.
source: Likewise, another key residue in DCLK1.2, Lys 692, anchors the tail to the catalytic domain through directional salt bridges with the conserved aspartates (Asp 511 and Asp 533) in the HRD and DFG motifs (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: These interactions are not observed in DCLK1.1 simulations because Lys 692 is substituted to a histidine (His 689), which is unable to form a corresponding interaction with the catalytic domain.
source: These interactions are not observed in DCLK1.1 simulations because Lys 692 is substituted to a histidine (His 689), which is unable to form a corresponding interaction with the catalytic domain (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: T688A or T688E mutations slightly destabilize the tail relative to WT DCLK1.2.
source: We also evaluated the effects of T688A (non-phosphorylated) or T688E (phosphomimetic) mutations through DCLK1 MD simulations and found that the two mutations slightly destabilize the tail relative to WT.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: Three replicates of the T688A and T688E mutants show increased RMSF of the tail region relative to WT DCLK1.1.
source: Three replicates of the two mutants show increased RMSF of the tail region relative to WT DCLK1.1 (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: BPPS analysis revealed DCLK-specific constraints in different regions of the kinase domain, most notably, the ATP-binding G-loop, N terminus of the C-helix, the activation loop, and C-terminus of the F-helix.
source: BPPS analysis revealed DCLK-specific constraints in different regions of the kinase domain, most notably, the ATP-binding G-loop, N terminus of the C-helix, the activation loop, and C-terminus of the F-helix (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by BPPS analysis data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Asp 398, Asn 400, and Ala 402 in the G-loop are unique to DCLKs.
source: In particular, Asp 398, Asn 400, and Ala 402 are unique to DCLKs as the corresponding residues are strikingly different in other CAMKs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Asp 398 is typically a charged residue (K/R) in other CAMKs.
source: Asp 398 is typically a charged residue (K/R) in other CAMKs while Asn 400 and Ala 402 are typically hydrophobic and polar residues, respectively (see residue frequencies in background alignment; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 6B.

claim: Asn 400 and Ala 402 are typically hydrophobic and polar residues, respectively, in other CAMKs.
source: Asp 398 is typically a charged residue (K/R) in other CAMKs while Asn 400 and Ala 402 are typically hydrophobic and polar residues, respectively (see residue frequencies in background alignment; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 6B.

claim: Both Asn 400 and Asp 398 make direct interactions with residues in the C-tail either in the crystal structure or MD simulations.
source: Notably, both Asn 400 and Asp 398 make direct interactions with residues in the C-tail either in the crystal structure or MD simulations (see below).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on structural and MD simulation analysis.

claim: DCLK conserved residues in the C-helix and activation loop tether the C-terminal tail to functional regions of the kinase core.
source: Likewise, DCLK conserved residues in the C-helix and activation loop tether the C-terminal tail to functional regions of the kinase core, suggesting co-option of the DCLK catalytic domain to uniquely interact with the flanking cis-regulatory tail.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claim: A unique region (682–688 in DCLK1.2) docks into the ATP-binding pocket through both hydrophobic and hydrogen-bonding interactions.
source: The most stable segment of the C-tail based on the B-factor and RMSF fluctuations in MD simulations is a unique region (682–688 in DCLK1.2) that docks into the ATP-binding pocket through both hydrophobic and hydrogen-bonding interactions.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on MD simulation analysis.

claim: This peptide segment mimics the physiological ATP ligand, and stabilizes the catalytic domain through 'completion' of the hydrophobic catalytic spine.
source: Remarkably, this peptide segment mimics the physiological ATP ligand, and stabilizes the catalytic domain through 'completion' of the hydrophobic catalytic spine (Figure 7A; Zheng et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by structural analysis in Figure 7A and a citation.

claim: The residues that mimic adenosine and complete the C-spine of DCLK1 are Val 682, Val 684, and Ile 685.
source: The residues that mimic adenosine and complete the C-spine of DCLK1 are Val 682, Val 684, and Ile 685 (PDB: 6KYQ), which are part of the alpha-helix that docks to the ATP-binding pocket (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by structural data in Figure 7B.

claim: These C-tail residues (Val 682, Val 684, and Ile 685) are uniquely vertebrate DCLK1-specific pattern constraints.
source: Interestingly, based on our BPPS analyses, these C-tail residues are uniquely vertebrate DCLK1-specific pattern constraints.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on BPPS analysis.

claim: Thr 687 and Thr 688 are at the tail end of the alpha-helix in DCLK1.2.
source: At the tail end of this alpha-helix are two Thr residues, Thr 687 and Thr 688.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on structural analysis.

claim: Thr 687 and Thr 688 mark the beginning of exon 17, and are one of the key variations between human DCLK1 isoforms, found only in DCLK1.2 variants.
source: As previously noted, these Thr residues mark the beginning of exon 17, and are one of the key variations between human DCLK1 isoforms, found only in DCLK1.2 variants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on genomic and sequence analysis.

claim: Thr 687 in DCLK1.2 caps the stable alpha-helix that extends the C-spine.
source: Structural analysis and MD simulations reveal that Thr 687 in DCLK1.2 caps the stable alpha-helix that extends the C-spine (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by structural and MD simulation data in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Upon phosphorylation, Thr 688 in DCLK1.2 can mimic the gamma phosphate of ATP by maintaining a stable hydrogen bonding distance with the backbone of the second glycine of the G-loop (G399).
source: Upon phosphorylation, Thr 688 in DCLK1.2 can mimic the gamma phosphate of ATP by maintaining a stable hydrogen bonding distance with the backbone of the second glycine of the G-loop (G399) (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by structural and MD simulation data in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The sidechain of Asn 400 further stabilizes the phosphate group in pThr 688 through hydrogen bonding.
source: We additionally observe that the sidechain of Asn 400, a DCLK-specific G-loop constraint, further stabilizes the phosphate group in pThr 688 through hydrogen bonding.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on structural analysis.

claim: Thr 688 is unique to DCLK1.2.
source: As previously described, Thr 688 is unique to DCLK1.2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The lack of Thr 688 in DCK1.1 is correlated with increased RMSF and instability of the ATP-mimic segment in isoform 1 MDs.
source: The lack of this functional site in DCK1.1 is correlated with increased RMSF and instability of the ATP-mimic segment in isoform 1 MDs (Figure 5C–D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 5C-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MD analysis of DCLK1.2 and a phosphothreonine-containing DCLK1.2 demonstrates reduced C-tail fluctuations.
source: Comparatively, MD analysis of DCLK1.2 and a phosphothreonine-containing DCLK1.2 demonstrates reduced C-tail fluctuations, suggesting the potential regulatory involvement of Thr 688 phosphorylation for further modulation of the autoinhibited conformation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), consistent with previous findings (Agulto et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by MD simulation data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and a citation.

claim: Mutation of Asp 398 or Asn 400 in the Gly-rich loop are by themselves insufficient to destabilize DCLK1.2.
source: The ΔTm values obtained (Figure 8C) demonstrate that mutation of Asp 398 or Asn 400 in the Gly-rich loop are by themselves insufficient to destabilize DCLK1.2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by thermal stability data in Figure 8C.

claim: Dual mutation of the hydrophobic pair of Val 682 and Val 684 residues to Thr resulted in a pronounced reduction in DCLK1.2 thermal stability.
source: In marked contrast, dual mutation of the hydrophobic pair of Val 682 and Val 684 residues to Thr, or mutation of the acidic tail residue Asp 691, resulted in a pronounced reduction in DCLK1.2 thermal stability.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on thermal stability assay data.

claim: Mutation of the acidic tail residue Asp 691 resulted in a pronounced reduction in DCLK1.2 thermal stability.
source: In marked contrast, dual mutation of the hydrophobic pair of Val 682 and Val 684 residues to Thr, or mutation of the acidic tail residue Asp 691, resulted in a pronounced reduction in DCLK1.2 thermal stability.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on thermal stability assay data.

claim: The recorded Tm values for V682T/V684T and D691A mutations closely resembled the Tm of DCLK1cat.
source: Moreover, the recorded Tm values for these latter two mutations quite closely resembled the Tm of DCLK1cat (which lacks the C-tail entirely), which is consistent with the uncoupling of the C-tail and a commensurate decrease in thermal stability associated with loss of this interaction.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on thermal stability assay data.

claim: Both DCLK1.1short (351–703) and DCLK1.1long (351–729) variants possess robust catalytic activity.
source: Although partially diminished in relation to DCLK1cat, both DCLK1.1short (351–703) and DCLK1.1long (351–729) variants possess robust catalytic activity.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on kinase activity assay data.

claim: Both C-tail containing variants of DCLK1.1 exhibited lower affinity for ATP (inferred from KM[ATP] for peptide phosphorylation).
source: Interestingly, both C-tail containing variants of DCLK1.1 (and particularly DCLK1.1351-729) exhibited lower affinity for ATP (inferred from KM[ATP] for peptide phosphorylation), which is consistent with partial occlusion of the ATP-binding pocket (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by kinase activity assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The detectable kinase activity for short (351–703) or long (351–740) DCLK1.2 proteins was significantly blunted compared to DCLK1cat, exhibiting just ~5% of the activity of the catalytic domain alone.
source: In marked contrast, the detectable kinase activity for short (351–703) or long (351–740) DCLK1.2 proteins was significantly blunted compared to DCLK1cat, exhibiting just ~5% of the activity of the catalytic domain alone, and consistently, the calculated KM[ATP] was ~4-fold higher compared to the catalytic domain lacking the C-tail.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on kinase activity assay data.

claim: The calculated KM[ATP] for DCLK1.2 proteins was ~4-fold higher compared to the catalytic domain lacking the C-tail.
source: In marked contrast, the detectable kinase activity for short (351–703) or long (351–740) DCLK1.2 proteins was significantly blunted compared to DCLK1cat, exhibiting just ~5% of the activity of the catalytic domain alone, and consistently, the calculated KM[ATP] was ~4-fold higher compared to the catalytic domain lacking the C-tail.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on kinase activity assay data.

claim: Quantitative tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) analysis of site-specific autophosphorylation within DCLK1.1short and DCLK1.2short demonstrate a marked reduction in the site-specific abundance of phosphate in DCLK1.2 when compared to DCLK1.1 at two separate sites (S438 and S660).
source: We also utilized autophosphorylation as a proxy for overall kinase activity. Quantitative tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) analysis of site-specific autophosphorylation within DCLK1.1short and DCLK1.2short demonstrate a marked reduction in the site-specific abundance of phosphate in DCLK1.2 when compared to DCLK1.1 at two separate sites that could be directly and accurately quantified by MS (S438 and S660, DCLK1.1 relative abundance set to 1, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by MS/MS data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: LC-MS/MS indicated that several autophosphorylation sites identified in isoform 1 were absent in DCLK1.2 (Ser 683 and Thr 692).
source: LC-MS/MS also indicated that several autophosphorylation sites identified in isoform 1 were absent in DCLK1.2 (Ser 683 and Thr 692, the latter of which is an amino acid that is unique to the C-tail of DCLK1.1, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: DCLK1.2 D398A was activated some fivefold when compared to the WT form.
source: Interestingly, amino acid substitutions in the G-loop or the C-tail of DCLK1.2 designed to subvert C-tail and ATP site interactions also had major effects on DCLK1.2 phosphorylation and catalytic activity. DCLK1.2 D398A was activated some fivefold when compared to the WT form, whereas DCLK1.2 N400A was almost as active as the DCLK1cat.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on kinase activity assay data.

claim: DCLK1.2 N400A was almost as active as the DCLK1cat.
source: Interestingly, amino acid substitutions in the G-loop or the C-tail of DCLK1.2 designed to subvert C-tail and ATP site interactions also had major effects on DCLK1.2 phosphorylation and catalytic activity. DCLK1.2 D398A was activated some fivefold when compared to the WT form, whereas DCLK1.2 N400A was almost as active as the DCLK1cat.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on kinase activity assay data.

claim: DCLK1.2 V682T/V684T and D691A proteins were much more active than the WT form of DCLK1.2.
source: Consistently, DCLK1.2 V682T/V684T and D691A proteins were also much more active than the WT form of DCLK1.2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on kinase activity assay data.

claim: Kinetic analysis confirmed higher Vmax (but broadly similar KM[ATP]) values for DCLK1.2 D398A and V682T/V684T relative to the WT protein.
source: Kinetic analysis also confirmed higher Vmax (but broadly similar KM[ATP]) values for DCLK1.2 D398A and V682T/V684T relative to the WT protein (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by kinetic analysis data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Comprehensive LC-MS/MS phosphosite mapping revealed a marked increase in the total number of phosphorylated amino acids in all of the mutant DCLK1.2 proteins, consistent with the enhanced catalytic activity of these proteins when compared to WT DCLK1.2.
source: Moreover, comprehensive LC-MS/MS phosphosite mapping revealed a marked increase in the total number of phosphorylated amino acids in all of the mutant DCLK1.2 proteins, consistent with the enhanced catalytic activity of these proteins when compared to WT DCLK1.2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: DCLK1cat (351–686), DCLK1.1short (351–703) and DCLK1.1long (351–729) proteins all behaved similarly in the presence of either Mg:ATP or DCLK1-IN-1, inducing marked stabilization.
source: DCLK1cat (351–686), DCLK1.1short (351–703) and DCLK1.1long (351–729) proteins all behaved similarly in the presence of either Mg:ATP or DCLK1-IN-1, inducing marked stabilization.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on thermal stability assay data.

claim: DCLK1.2short (351–703) or DCLK1.2long (351–740) proteins registered negligible thermal shifts in the presence of Mg:ATP or DCLK1-IN-1.
source: In contrast, DCLK1.2short (351–703) or DCLK1.2long (351–740) proteins registered negligible thermal shifts in the presence of the same concentration of either ligand, which is in line with the C-tail tightly occupying the ATP-binding site and obstructing their binding.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on thermal stability assay data.

claim: D398A and N400A DCLK1.2 were markedly destabilized in the presence of either Mg:ATP or DCLK-IN-1.
source: Remarkably, D398A and N400A DCLK1.2, whose high basal Tm values (compared to DCLK1cat) are consistent with stabilization by docking of the C-tail within the kinase domain, were markedly destabilized in the presence of either ligand.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on thermal stability assay data.

claim: DCLK1.2 V682T/V684T and D691A were both stabilized in a ligand-dependent manner to a similar degree to that observed for DCLK1cat and DCLK1.1 proteins.
source: Finally, DCLK1.2 V682T/V684T and D691A, which exhibit lower basal Tm values than the WT protein (indicating a loss of tail interaction), were both stabilized in a ligand-dependent manner to a similar degree to that observed for DCLK1cat and DCLK1.1 proteins (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by thermal stability assay data in Figure 8E.

claim: The C-tail section of DCLK1.2 can both stabilize the canonical DCLK kinase domain and inhibit kinase activity much more effectively than that of DCLK1.1.
source: Collectively, these observations clearly demonstrate that the C-tail section of DCLK1.2 can both stabilize the canonical DCLK kinase domain and inhibit kinase activity (by impeding the binding and structural coordination of Mg:ATP) much more effectively than that of DCLK1.1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Targeted mutational analysis of key contact residues in DCLK1.2 shows that this is a consequence of specific amino acid interactions that are absent in DCLK1.1 due to alternative-splicing and subsequent sequence variation.
source: Our targeted mutational analysis of key contact residues in DCLK1.2 also clearly shows that this is a consequence of specific amino acid interactions that are absent in DCLK1.1 due to alternative-splicing and subsequent sequence variation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on mutational analysis data.

claim: The DCLK C-tail can be classified into six functional segments based on interactions with different regions of the catalytic domain and their conservation between the C-tail splice variants.
source: We synthesized our experimental findings by classifying the DCLK C-tail into six functional segments, based on interactions with different regions of the catalytic domain and their conservation between the C-tail splice variants in our analysis (Figure 9):
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 9.

claim: An ATP-mimetic peptide segment (residues 682–688 in DCLK1.2) readily mimics physiological ATP binding by completing the C-spine in the nucleotide-binding site.
source: First is an ATP-mimetic peptide segment (residues 682–688 in DCLK1.2) that readily mimics physiological ATP binding by completing the C-spine in the nucleotide-binding site.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on structural and functional analysis.

claim: The inhibitory peptide contains a phosphorylatable Thr residue, which sits adjacent to the highly characteristic Gly-rich loop (GDGNFA, residues 396–402).
source: The inhibitory peptide also contains a phosphorylatable Thr residue, which sits adjacent to the highly characteristic Gly-rich loop (GDGNFA, residues 396–402).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on structural analysis.

claim: A pseudosubstrate mimic (residues 692–701) interacts with the acidic HRD and DFG Asp sidechains and docks in the substrate pocket occluding substrate access.
source: Second, we define a pseudosubstrate mimic (residues 692–701), which interacts with the acidic HRD and DFG Asp sidechains and docks in the substrate pocket occluding substrate access.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on structural and functional analysis.

claim: An IDS (residues 702–749) packs dynamically against DCLK conserved residues in the kinase activation loop.
source: Third, at the C-terminus of the tail lies an IDS (residues 702–749, Figure 9—figure supplement 1), which packs dynamically against DCLK conserved residues in the kinase activation loop.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: A CAMK-tether (residues 654–664) is a set of residues that pack against a CAMK-specific insert in the C-lobe.
source: Fourth, at the beginning of the C-tail lies a CAMK-tether (residues 654–664), a set of residues that pack against a CAMK-specific insert in the C-lobe.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on structural analysis.

claim: A highly dynamic pseudosubstrate region (residues 672–678) occludes the substrate pocket and will thus interfere with substrate phosphorylation.
source: Fifth, this is followed by a highly dynamic pseudosubstrate region (residues 672–678) that occludes the substrate pocket and will thus interfere with substrate phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on structural and functional analysis.

claim: A transient beta-strand is formed in DCLK1.2 through amino acid-specific sequences that help modulate and potentially strengthen binding of the C-tail in this isoform.
source: Sixth, a transient beta-strand is formed in DCLK1.2 through amino acid-specific sequences that help modulate and potentially strengthen binding of the C-tail in this isoform (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Co-evolution of the unique C-tail with the catalytic domain is the central hallmark of DCLK functional divergence.
source: Collectively, these segments and their associated interaction sites demonstrate that co-evolution of the unique C-tail with the catalytic domain is the central hallmark of DCLK functional divergence, and that changes in these segments possess the ability to 'supercharge' catalytic output of the kinase.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is based on comprehensive analysis of DCLK structure and function.

claim: The variable C-terminal segments of the tail might contribute to isoform-specific functional specialization.
source: In particular, the variable C-terminal segments of the tail might contribute to isoform-specific functional specialization.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is speculative based on structural and functional analysis.

claim: Isoform-specific variability provides additional nuance to regulatory and catalytic signaling events and may even contribute to differences in cellular localization and tissue-specific activity.
source: Isoform-specific variability provides additional nuance to regulatory and catalytic signaling events and may even contribute to differences in cellular localization (e.g. cytoplasm or nucleoplasm) and tissue-specific activity, enabling contextual DCLK regulation through these modular sequence segments.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is speculative based on structural and functional analysis.
